newsitem.title: SPAIN: Jordan's King saddened by attack, vows peace.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's King saddened by attack, vows peace.

text.p: Jordan's King Hussein expressed regret, sorrow and anger at the killing of seven Israeli schoolgirls by a Jordanian gunman on Thursday and vowed to work the rest of his life for Middle East peace.

Hussein, who had warned this week that plans to expand Israeli settlements in Arab East Jerusalem could spark violence, defended himself against accusations by Israeli ministers that his words were somehow connected to the attack.
"I can assure you I shall do everything I can as long as I live to leave behind a legacy of peace between (Arabs and Jews) for all time," Hussein told reporters during a private visit to Spain.

Seven Israeli teenager girls were killed and at least six wounded by a Jordanian soldier who sprayed automatic gunfire at a group on a field trip to a Jordanian border site nicknamed "The Island of Peace".
It was the bloodiest attack by a Jordanian soldier on the Israel-Jordan frontier in many years.

"This is something that is aimed I feel at me, at my children, at the people of Jordan and the Jordanian army," Hussein told reporters at a Madrid palace just before bidding farewell to Spanish King Juan Carlos.
Hussein cut short his trip to Spain and postponed a planned subsequent visit to the United States to fly home and deal with the fresh crisis in Middle East peace.
The king wrote to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday accusing him of pushing Arabs and Israelis towards "an abyss of bloodshed and disaster".
Before the attack, Arabs had warned Israel its plan to build housing in East Jerusalem plunged the whole U.S.-sponsored peace drive into crisis.
"It was fully in my responsibility to warn that we have come too far," Hussein said in defence of his letter.
Israel's Education Minister Zevulun Hammer suggested after the attack that King Hussein should not have spoken out about possible violence.
"Perhaps the conclusion is that the king must hold his tongue so that a soldier doesn't take his words to mean more than he intended," Hammer told Israel's army radio.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said the gunman may have been provoked by disparaging comments about Israel but he denied he was referring to the king's letter.
"Who knows...how many of these gun-toting lunatics are waiting for the green light in the form of a remark in which Israel is described the way it is being described today," Levy said.
Hussein expressed his sorrow at what he called a tragic loss of innocent lives.
"I sympathise with the families. I wish I could see them all and share with them in their sorrow," he said.
